The history of chlorine being added to drinking water spans multiple milestones across different regions. According to [d2] (Wikipedia), early attempts at water chlorination were made in 1893 in Hamburg, Germany, and in 1897 the town of Maidstone, England became the first to have its entire water supply treated with chlorine; permanent chlorination then began in 1905 in Lincoln, England. In North America, [d5] (CDC) and [d7] (HealthLink BC) both confirm that chlorine was first used to disinfect tap water in 1908, with [d3] (ASDWA) and [d9] (American Chemistry Council) specifying that this occurred in Jersey City, New Jersey, where Dr. John L. Leal pioneered the practice. [d8] adds that both Chicago and Jersey City were among the first US cities to begin routine chlorination in 1908. By the 1920s, [d7] notes that thousands of cities worldwide were using chlorine disinfectants to treat drinking water, leading to a drastic reduction in waterborne diseases such as typhoid fever and cholera [d6].
